messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Hotel Manager
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 62

He is a 67-year-old North American man who has spent most of his adult life in hospitality, and even now, as a hotel manager, he carries himself with the practiced calm of someone used to smoothing over problems before guests ever notice them. For years, his work has depended on being approachable, alert, and in control. That part of him did not change quickly after the mugging, but the confidence behind it did.

The robbery happens on an evening when he is leaving work later than usual. He is tired, thinking about unfinished paperwork and an argument with a vendor, and he takes the same route he has used many times before. He remembers the ordinary details first: the cold air, the glow of storefront lights, the weight of his keys in his pocket. Then two men move toward him too quickly. One demands his wallet. The other blocks his path. He tries to make sense of it, tries to keep his voice steady the way he would with an upset guest, but the situation has already become something else. He feels the sharp, humiliating panic of not knowing what they want next. There is a shove, a threat, a hand reaching toward him, and the whole scene becomes fixed in his memory in fragments—his own breathing, the sound of his shoes scuffing the pavement, the men’s faces too close and then suddenly not.

In the days afterward, he tells himself he is fine. That is his habit. He has spent a lifetime being the person who handles things. He returns to work, answers calls, checks reservations, and speaks to his staff in the same measured tone. But his body does not believe him. At night he lies awake with his heart racing, replaying the moment of the mugging in exacting detail. He starts hearing sounds before he falls asleep—the hum of traffic, a car door slamming outside, footsteps in the hallway—and each one sharpens his body into readiness. He wakes easily and often, sometimes from dreams he cannot fully remember but that leave him sweating and disoriented. In the morning he feels drained, as if he has already worked a full shift before he gets out of bed.

Walking outside becomes a calculation. He avoids the street where it happened and begins parking farther away, then wonders whether he should be going out at all after dark. He keeps checking over his shoulder. If someone approaches too quickly in a lobby or on the sidewalk, his whole body tightens and he feels the old surge of helplessness before he can think it through. At work, he still performs his duties, but he is less patient and more guarded. He notices himself scanning entrances, watching people’s hands, lingering near exits without meaning to. In meetings, he has trouble following what people are saying because part of him is always somewhere else, listening for danger.

He becomes easily startled. A sudden knock on his office door makes him jump in a way that embarrasses him. He begins to avoid discussing the assault with his wife because he does not want to see fear in her face, and because saying it aloud seems to make it more real. Instead he grows quieter at home. He sits through dinner but does not fully engage. His wife notices that he is less interested in plans they used to make together, less willing to drive unfamiliar routes or go downtown for an evening out. He tells himself he is simply being practical, but there is a shrinking in his life that he cannot ignore. Places that once felt ordinary now seem charged with risk.

As time passes, he also carries a deep frustration with himself. He does not like feeling vulnerable. He has worked in hotels long enough to know how quickly an environment can shift from controlled to chaotic, yet he is still ashamed that a brief street robbery has altered the way he moves through the world. He thinks about strength in the old-fashioned way, as endurance, and he resents that sleep, concentration, and ease have become difficult. Some days he feels numb and detached, as if he is watching his own life from a little distance. Other days he is flooded with tension and anger, especially when he feels trapped or rushed.

By the time he comes to therapy, the event is no longer new, but it remains active in him. He continues to work, continues to manage, continues to show up, yet his days are organized around not being caught off guard. He speaks about the robbery in a controlled voice, but his hands move restlessly as he describes it, and there are moments when he goes silent, staring ahead as though the scene is unfolding again just beyond his reach.
